proofs.proof_tex:
Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), the matrix \(A\) is lower triangular, it obeys the graph-support zero restrictions, \(\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\), the matrix \(D\) is diagonal with \(D_{ii}>0\), and
\[
 A^m=B,
 \qquad
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top .
\]

We first identify the diagonal of \(A\).  Multiplication of lower-triangular matrices shows that the \((i,i)\) entry of a product is the product of the \((i,i)\) entries.  Induction on \(r\) therefore gives
\[
 (A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r,
 \qquad
 B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m.
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass{:}odd\mbox{-}factor}\), \(m\) is odd.  For real \(x<y\),
\[
 y^m-x^m=(y-x)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y^{m-1-k}x^k>0;
\]
indeed, if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same sign this is immediate after factoring their absolute values, while if \(x<0<y\), then \(x^m<0<y^m\).  Thus \(x\mapsto x^m\) is injective on \(\mathbb R\), and every compatible pair must have the same diagonal
\[
 A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m},
\]
where the right side denotes the unique real odd root.

We next recover the strict lower triangle by induction on the endpoint gap \(g=i-j\).  Suppose that all entries whose gaps are smaller than \(g\) have already been fixed.  If \(j\to i\) is allowed by \(G\), the result \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives
\[
 B_{ij}=A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Every off-diagonal factor appearing in the remainder has endpoint gap strictly less than \(g\), so the induction hypothesis and the graph-support zeros determine \(R_{ij,m}(A)\).  The theorem's noncollision premise says that \((A_{ii},A_{jj})\ne(0,0)\) on every allowed edge.  The odd part of \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\) consequently yields
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})>0.
\]
Division is valid and forces
\[
 A_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.
\]
If \(j\to i\) is not allowed, \(\mathrm{ass{:}graph\mbox{-}support}\) instead forces \(A_{ij}=0\); and \(\mathrm{ass{:}lower\mbox{-}triangular}\) forces \(A_{ij}=0\) when \(i<j\).  Starting with \(g=1\) and continuing through \(g=d-1\) therefore determines every entry of \(A\).  In particular, two elements of the compatible fiber have the same transition matrix.

Fix this uniquely determined \(A\).  Because \(D\) is diagonal, the \((i,i)\) coordinate of the covariance equation is
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(A^r)_{ij}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
Every power of a lower-triangular matrix is lower triangular, so \((A^r)_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\), and the diagonal identity above gives \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  Hence
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
  +\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
The coefficient
\[
 s_i:=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
\]
is at least its \(r=0\) summand, namely one.  Induction over \(i=1,\ldots,d\) therefore permits division by \(s_i\) and uniquely gives
\[
 D_{ii}
 =\frac{Q_{ii}-\displaystyle\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}
                 \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}}
        {\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}}.
\]
Thus two members of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) also have the same \(D\), proving that a nonempty compatible fiber is a singleton.

It remains to prove the claimed exact compatibility test, including sufficiency.  For an input satisfying the theorem's odd-root noncollision condition, construct a candidate \(A^\star\) by the displayed diagonal and allowed-edge recursions, set all structurally forbidden coordinates to zero, and then construct diagonal \(D^\star\) by the covariance recursion.  The diagonal equations \(((A^\star)^m)_{ii}=B_{ii}\) hold by the odd-root construction.  On each allowed edge, the path-expansion identity and the defining recursion give \(((A^\star)^m)_{ij}=B_{ij}\).  Therefore \((A^\star)^m=B\) holds exactly when it also holds at every remaining, structurally forbidden coordinate.  The diagonal covariance equations hold by construction, and the full covariance check is exactly
\[
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^\star)^rD^\star((A^\star)^r)^\top.
\]
The matrix \(A^\star\) has the required triangular and graph zeros by construction.  Its stability condition in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) is exactly \(\max_i|A^\star_{ii}|<1\).  Since \(D^\star\) is diagonal, \(D^\star\succ0\) is equivalent to \(D^\star_{ii}>0\) for every \(i\).  Consequently the stability check, positivity of every recovered innovation variance, the remaining coordinates of \((A^\star)^m=B\), and the complete covariance equation together imply every condition in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), and hence are sufficient.  Conversely, if a compatible pair exists, the preceding uniqueness argument shows that it equals \((A^\star,D^\star)\); the definition of the fiber then makes every listed check necessary.  This proves the stated if-and-only-if criterion for the recursively produced candidate.

Finally, \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\) maps each compatible structural pair to the direct structural transfer
\[
 z\longmapsto \frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}.
\]
This is the causal target specified by the fine-grid structural equation, whereas \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is its observed-law compatible image.  For \(|z|=1\), stability implies \(|A_{vv}z|=|A_{vv}|<1\), so the denominator is nonzero.  Since the compatible parameter fiber is a singleton, its image is the singleton \(\{h_{uv}\}\).  Thus the causal transfer is identified from \((B,Q,G,m)\), rather than being equated to an observed-law functional by definition.

For an exact regular stress test, take \(d=2\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) contain \(1\to2\), and set
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\[2pt]1/4&1/3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D=I_2.
\]
Both endpoint persistences are nonzero and \(A\) is stable.  There is no indirect path, and direct multiplication, equivalently the path expansion, gives
\[
 B_{11}=\frac18,
 \qquad B_{22}=\frac1{27},
 \qquad B_{21}=\frac14 C_3\!\left(\frac13,\frac12\right)
 =\frac14\left(\frac19+\frac16+\frac14\right)
 =\frac{19}{144}.
\]
Since \(C_3(1/3,1/2)=19/36\), the recursion returns \(A_{21}=1/4\).  For the generated coarse covariance, direct calculation gives
\[
 Q_{11}=\frac{21}{16},
 \qquad
 Q_{22}=\frac{61}{576}+\frac{91}{81}.
\]
The innovation recursion consequently returns
\[
 D_{11}=\frac{21/16}{1+1/4+1/16}=1,
 \qquad
 D_{22}=\frac{Q_{22}-(1/16+25/576)}{1+1/9+1/81}=1.
\]
Thus it recovers the transfer \(z/[4(1-z/3)]\).

The noncollision condition is load-bearing.  Keep \(d=2\), \(m=3\), and the same allowed edge, and for \(q_1,q_2>0\) define
\[
 A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ a&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1),
 \qquad
 |a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1}.
\]
Then \(D(a)\succ0\), \(A(a)^2=0\), and hence
\[
 A(a)^3=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
 =D(a)+A(a)D(a)A(a)^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
All these stable Gaussian fine-grid models therefore induce the same pair \((B,Q)=(0,\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2))\), but their transfers are \(h_{12}(z)=az\), an open interval of distinct functions.  Here both endpoint persistences vanish and \(C_3(0,0)=0\), so this example violates precisely the noncollision premise used for division and shows why that premise cannot be dropped from the singleton conclusion.

Fix the effective \(K\)-valued matrices \(B,Q\), the supplied graph \(G\), and the known integer \(m\geq 2\).  Define the index set
\[
 \mathcal I_G
 =\{(i,i):i\in V\}\cup
   \{(i,j):j<i\text{ and }j\to i\text{ in }G\}.
\]
For every \((i,j)\in\mathcal I_G\), introduce a real variable \(a_{ij}\), and introduce real variables \(d_1,\ldots,d_d\).  Let \(\widetilde A(a)\) have entry \(a_{ij}\) on \(\mathcal I_G\) and zero elsewhere, and let \(\widetilde D(d)=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_d)\).  Thus the lower-triangular and graph-support restrictions in \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) are imposed by the coordinate parametrization itself.

Consider the finite system
\[
 \bigl[\widetilde A(a)^m\bigr]_{ij}=B_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{1}
\]
\[
 \left[\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\widetilde A(a)^r\widetilde D(d)
                    \bigl(\widetilde A(a)^r\bigr)^\top\right]_{ij}
 =Q_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 -1<a_{ii}<1\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad d_i>0\quad(i\in V).                                        \tag{3}
\]
Every left-hand side in (1)--(2) is a polynomial in finitely many variables with coefficients in \(K\), by \(\mathrm{ass{:}effective\mbox{-}input}\).  Since \(\widetilde A(a)\) is triangular,
\[
 \det\!\bigl(\lambda I-\widetilde A(a)\bigr)
   =\prod_{i=1}^d(\lambda-a_{ii}),
 \qquad
 \rho\!\bigl(\widetilde A(a)\bigr)=\max_i|a_{ii}|.
\]
Consequently the first collection of strict inequalities in (3) is equivalent to stability.  Moreover, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R^d\),
\[
 x^\top\widetilde D(d)x=\sum_{i=1}^d d_i x_i^2>0
\]
if and only if every \(d_i>0\).  Hence the second collection in (3) is equivalent to \(\widetilde D(d)\succ0\).  It follows from \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) that
\[
 (a,d)\longmapsto\bigl(\widetilde A(a),\widetilde D(d)\bigr)         \tag{4}
\]
is a bijection from the realization of (1)--(3) onto \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  In particular, this encoding neither adds boundary points nor replaces strict positivity or strict stability by their closures.

For a triangular matrix, the diagonal part of (1) is
\[
 a_{ii}^{\,m}=B_{ii},\qquad i\in V.                                 \tag{5}
\]
The effective arithmetic, sign tests, and real-root isolation supplied by the definition of \(K\) enumerate the real roots of each equation (5) and decide the strict inequalities in (3).  There is exactly one real root of \(x^m=b\) when \(m\) is odd; when \(m\) is even there are zero, one, or two real roots according as \(b<0\), \(b=0\), or \(b>0\).  Thus there are finitely many surviving diagonal branches, all represented exactly in \(K\).  If none survives, (4) shows that the compatible fiber is empty.

Fix one surviving branch and process off-diagonal pairs \((v,u)\) in increasing order of \(v-u\), as prescribed by \(\mathrm{def{:}graph\mbox{-}recursion}\).  The lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives
\[
 a_{vu}C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})
   =B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}\!\bigl(\widetilde A(a)\bigr).                  \tag{6}
\]
Every off-diagonal coordinate occurring on the right-hand side of (6) has smaller endpoint gap.  The diagonal entries in
\[
 c_{vu}:=C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})                                        \tag{7}
\]
are fixed on the branch, so \(c_{vu}\in K\).  The lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\), together with the exact sign tests in \(K\), decides whether \(c_{vu}=0\).  In particular, the odd-factor case \(a_{vv}=a_{uu}=0\) and the even-factor case \(a_{vv}=-a_{uu}\) are retained as singular cases.

If \(u\to v\) is graph-allowed and \(c_{vu}\neq0\), equation (6) is equivalent to the unique substitution
\[
 a_{vu}
 =\frac{B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}\!\bigl(\widetilde A(a)\bigr)}{c_{vu}}.     \tag{8}
\]
This is the only division in the recursion, and it is made only after the nonzero test.  Because \(c_{vu}^{-1}\in K\) is a fixed coefficient on the branch, and because all previously eliminated coordinates are polynomials over \(K\) in the coordinates retained so far, substitution of (8) into later transition and covariance equations again produces polynomials over \(K\) in the residual variables; it introduces no variable denominator.  If \(c_{vu}=0\), the coordinate is not eliminated and the induced equation
\[
 B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}\!\bigl(\widetilde A(a)\bigr)=0                    \tag{9}
\]
is retained.  If the edge is forbidden, \(a_{vu}=0\) by the support parametrization and the transition equation (9) is likewise retained, regardless of the value of \(c_{vu}\).

Induction over the endpoint gap proves exactness of the recursion.  At a nonsingular allowed coordinate, every solution of the system before substitution must have the value (8), and every solution of the substituted system lifts uniquely by (8).  At a singular or forbidden coordinate, no variable or equation needed for compatibility is discarded.  After the finitely many pairs have been processed, all transition equations not used for an equivalent substitution, all covariance equations (2), and all strict inequalities (3) remain imposed after the accumulated substitutions.  Therefore, if \(\mathfrak R_b\) denotes the residual semialgebraic realization on diagonal branch \(b\), reconstruction gives
\[
 \mathcal S(B,Q;G)
   =\bigcup_b \operatorname{Rec}_b(\mathfrak R_b),                 \tag{10}
\]
where equality is literal, rather than equality only after topological or Zariski closure.

Each \(\mathfrak R_b\) is a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict polynomial inequalities over \(K\).  There are finitely many branches and finitely many variables.  The cited lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}effective\mbox{-}cad\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}sampling}\) therefore implies that CAD terminates on every branch, decides whether \(\mathfrak R_b\) is empty, and returns an exact represented point when it is nonempty.  By (10), all branch systems are empty if and only if \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\).  This proves termination, soundness, and completeness of the incompatibility output of \(\operatorname{Cert}_{uv,m,G}(B,Q)\).

It remains to prove that the other two outputs classify the transfer fiber exactly.  Suppose the compatible fiber is nonempty, and take two compatible points.  Write
\[
 p=A_{vu},\quad q=A_{vv},\qquad
 p'=A'_{vu},\quad q'=A'_{vv}.
\]
Stability gives \(|q|<1\) and \(|q'|<1\).  Hence, for every \(z\in\mathbb T\),
\[
 |qz|<1,\qquad |q'z|<1,
\]
so neither \(1-qz\) nor \(1-q'z\) vanishes; moreover \(z\neq0\).  Cross multiplication and cancellation of \(z\) are therefore valid, and the two transfers agree on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if
\[
 p(1-q'z)=p'(1-qz)\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb T.             \tag{11}
\]
The difference between the two sides of (11) is
\[
 (p-p')+(p'q-pq')z.                                                 \tag{12}
\]
Evaluating (12) at \(z=1\) and \(z=-1\) shows that it vanishes on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if both of its coefficients vanish.  Thus
\[
 h_{p,q}=h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p=p'\ \text{ and }\ pq'=p'q,                                     \tag{13}
\]
and, because all quantities are real,
\[
 h_{p,q}\neq h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Delta(p,q,p',q')
 :=(p-p')^2+(pq'-p'q)^2>0.                                         \tag{14}
\]
Equation (13) correctly identifies all pairs \((0,q)\) with the same zero transfer; equality of the coefficient pair itself is not required.

For each ordered pair of diagonal branches, take two copies of the corresponding complete residual systems and append the strict polynomial inequality (14), after reconstruction.  The finite union of these two-copy systems is feasible if and only if there exist two points of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) having unequal transfers, by (10), (14), \(\mathrm{def{:}pair\mbox{-}fiber}\), and \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\).  The cited CAD lemma decides this feasibility and, when it holds, supplies exact residual sample points.  Reconstruction produces attained pairs
\[
 (A,D),(A',D')\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)
\]
satisfying
\[
 (A_{vu}-A'_{vu})^2+
 (A_{vu}A'_{vv}-A'_{vu}A_{vv})^2>0.
\]
Their strict diagonal and innovation inequalities are inherited from their branch systems, so the witnesses are stable and have positive diagonal innovation covariance.  This proves soundness of the ambiguity output, while the feasibility equivalence proves its completeness.

If every two-copy system is infeasible, (14) says that every two compatible points yield the same transfer.  A sample from any nonempty one-copy branch then supplies \((p,q)\) and hence the common exact rational function
\[
 z\longmapsto\frac{pz}{1-qz}.
\]
Conversely, if \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is a singleton, no two-copy system can satisfy (14), so the certificate returns this common function.  This establishes both directions of the singleton assertion and, together with the incompatibility and ambiguity cases, proves the claimed trichotomy for the algorithm in \(\mathrm{def{:}certificate}\).

All advertised exceptional cases are included in these equivalences.  Zero diagonal roots are retained in (5) and are sent to the singular residual system whenever the divided difference vanishes.  A forbidden queried edge, or an allowed queried edge forced to zero by compatibility, is handled by (13).  Open and positive-dimensional fibers are handled directly by the cited CAD lemma with the strict inequalities (3).  Branch duplication or merger cannot affect the answer because (10) is a union and the two-copy test ranges over every ordered branch pair.  No rank, overlap, conditioning, boundary relaxation, or limiting premise is used, and no division is made without the explicit nonzero condition in (8).

For completeness, the first requested exact stress test is realized inside the encoded fiber.  Let \(d=2\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) contain \(1\to2\), and set \(B=0\) and \(Q=I_2\).  Define
\[
 A_{\pm}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ \pm\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D_{\pm}=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right).
\]
Then \(A_{\pm}^2=0\), and hence
\[
 A_{\pm}^3=0=B,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A_{\pm}^rD_{\pm}(A_{\pm}^r)^\top
 =D_{\pm}+A_{\pm}D_{\pm}A_{\pm}^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right)
  +\operatorname{diag}\!\left(0,\tfrac14\right)
 =I_2.
\]
Both points satisfy \(\rho(A_{\pm})=0<1\) and \(D_{\pm}\succ0\), while their transfers are \(z/2\) and \(-z/2\).  Thus the two-copy system contains stable, strictly positive, transfer-distinct witnesses rather than only boundary points, so exact CAD cannot return a singleton in this case.

For the second stress test, let \(d=2\), \(m=2\), and let \((A,D)\) be any compatible point with \(A_{21}\neq0\).  The support zeros and lower-triangular form are preserved by \(A\mapsto-A\), as are stability and positivity of \(D\), and
\[
 (-A)^2=A^2,
 \qquad
 D+(-A)D(-A)^\top=D+ADA^\top.
\]
Thus \((-A,D)\) is a second compatible point for the same \((B,Q)\).  With \(p=A_{21}\), \(q=A_{22}\), \(p'=-p\), and \(q'=-q\),
\[
 \Delta(p,q,-p,-q)
 =(2p)^2+\{p(-q)-(-p)q\}^2
 =4p^2>0.
\]
Hence every nonzero-edge two-variable \(m=2\) case retains the global sign pair, as required.

Write
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}
 (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)
\]
and let
\[
 \mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{uv,\mathrm{cor}}^{\partial}
 (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa).
\]
We first verify that the assertion is nonvacuous and that the theorem for
\(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) applies.  By
\(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}class}\),
every \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) belongs to
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\), the integer
\(m\) is odd, and
\[
 m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\geq\kappa\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\geq\kappa\quad(j\to i\in E).
 \tag{1}
\]
The definition \(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor}\) gives
\(V_{uv}^{G}\subseteq V\) and \(E_{uv}^{G}\subseteq E\).  Restricting the
two finite families of inequalities in \((1)\) to these subsets and using
\(\mathrm{def{:}corridor\mbox{-}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class}\)
therefore yields
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}\subseteq\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The hypotheses of the present theorem include the hypotheses of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}nonempty}\),
and its numerical condition is
\(\kappa\leq m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\).  That lemma consequently gives
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}\neq\varnothing.
 \tag{3}
\]
Thus the supremum in the claimed coverage statement is not over an empty
class.

We next compare the global and corridor estimators.  The global recursion in
\(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}estimator}\) and the corridor recursion in
\(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion}\) use the same real
odd-root operation on every diagonal coordinate in \(V_{uv}^{G}\).  Process
the corridor edges in increasing endpoint gap.  For a corridor edge
\(j\to i\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion\mbox{-}closure}\)
states that every diagonal coordinate and every strict edge entering
\(R_{ij,m}\) is in the corridor and that each such strict edge has smaller
endpoint gap.  Induction over the endpoint gap therefore shows that the two
recursions have the same remainder, numerator, and denominator at every
corridor update.  Hence, whenever both recursions are defined,
\[
 \widehat A^{\mathrm{global}}_{ij}
 =\widehat A^{\mathrm{cor}}_{ij}
 \quad(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}),
 \qquad
 \widehat A^{\mathrm{global}}_{ii}
 =\widehat A^{\mathrm{cor}}_{ii}
 \quad(i\in V_{uv}^{G}).
 \tag{4}
\]
Because \(u,v\in V_{uv}^{G}\) and \(u\to v\in E_{uv}^{G}\), substitution
of the coordinates \((v,u)\) and \((v,v)\) from \((4)\) into the transfer
formula gives
\[
 \widehat h_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{\widehat A^{\mathrm{global}}_{vu}z}
 {1-\widehat A^{\mathrm{global}}_{vv}z}
 =\frac{\widehat A^{\mathrm{cor}}_{vu}z}
 {1-\widehat A^{\mathrm{cor}}_{vv}z}
 =\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z),
 \qquad z\in\mathcal Z.
 \tag{5}
\]

On \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\), all population diagonal-root derivatives and
all population divided differences used by the global recursion have
absolute value at least \(\kappa>0\), by \((1)\).  The uniform moment
consistency underlying
\(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}wald\mbox{-}band}\), continuity
of matrix inversion at \(M_0\succ0\), and the finite recursive composition
therefore imply that, uniformly over \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\), the
probability tends to one that all empirical diagonal derivatives and divided
differences used by the global recursion have absolute value at least
\(\kappa/2\).  Denote this common regularity event by \(\mathcal E_n\).  Thus
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\mathcal E_n^c)\longrightarrow0,
 \tag{6}
\]
and \((5)\) holds on \(\mathcal E_n\).  Arbitrary definitions of either
estimator off \(\mathcal E_n\) cannot affect a uniform weak limit or a
coverage probability, by \((6)\).

The same induction also proves equality as rational maps on the common
regular neighborhood, not merely equality at the observed argument.
Differentiating that identity shows that the target rows of the global and
corridor Jacobians agree.  Since the corridor expression contains no
off-corridor coordinate, its derivatives with respect to all such coordinates
are zero.  The transfer differential is, directly from the quotient rule,
\[
 \mathrm d h_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
 +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}.
 \tag{7}
\]
The denominators in \((7)\) are nonzero because the stability margin gives
\(|A_{vv}z|\leq1-\gamma<1\) for \(z\in\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb T\).
It follows that the global delta-method covariance restricted to the stacked
target vector equals the corridor covariance.  Applying the identical
recursive Jacobian to the same positive-semidefinite Isserlis-series covariance
estimate also gives, on \(\mathcal E_n\),
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_h=\widehat\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}},
 \qquad
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 =\widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}.
 \tag{8}
\]

Now apply
\(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}wald\mbox{-}band}\).  Its
hypotheses hold by the hypotheses of the present theorem, and \((2)\) permits
restriction of every uniform assertion from \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) to
\(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  Equations \((5)\)--\((8)\) then replace the
corridor estimator, covariance, and critical value by their global
counterparts without changing the uniform limit.  This proves the asserted
centered Gaussian limit with differential \((7)\).  Finally, if
\(C_n^{\mathrm{cor}}(P)\) and \(C_n^{\mathrm{global}}(P)\) denote the two
simultaneous-coverage events, then \((5)\) and \((8)\) give
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \left|P\!\left(C_n^{\mathrm{global}}(P)\right)
       -P\!\left(C_n^{\mathrm{cor}}(P)\right)\right|
 \leq
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\mathcal E_n^c)
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
Combining this display with the corridor theorem and the inclusion \((2)\)
gives exactly
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \left|P\!\left(C_n^{\mathrm{global}}(P)\right)-(1-\alpha)\right|
 \longrightarrow0,
\]
which is the claimed simultaneous Wald coverage.

Fix a data-generating law \(P_\star\) in
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\), let
\((A_\star,D_\star)\) be its fine-grid parameters, and let
\((M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\) be its stationary coarse moments.  Define the
event
\[
 E_n:=\{(M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\}.
\]
We first verify that the true fine model is feasible for the inverse on this
event.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}lower\mbox{-}triangular}\), the characteristic
polynomial of \(A_\star\) is
\[
 \det(\lambda I_d-A_\star)
 =\prod_{i\in V}\{\lambda-(A_\star)_{ii}\}.
\]
Thus the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.  The stability-margin
condition contained in \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\) consequently
gives
\[
 \rho(A_\star)=\max_{i\in V}|(A_\star)_{ii}|
 \leq 1-\gamma<1.
\]
The stability premise of \(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\)
therefore holds.  That lemma gives \(M_{0\star}\succ0\),
\(B_\star=A_\star^m=M_{1\star}M_{0\star}^{-1}\), and
\(Q_\star=M_{0\star}-B_\star M_{0\star}B_\star^\top\), where
\(Q_\star=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_\star^rD_\star(A_\star^r)^\top\).  Multiplication
of the first moment identity on the right by \(M_{0\star}\), followed by
substitution in the second one, yields the two defining moment equations
\[
 M_{1\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star},
 \qquad
 M_{0\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star}(A_\star^m)^\top
 +\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_\star^rD_\star(A_\star^r)^\top.
\]
Membership in \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\) separately supplies
the lower-triangular zero restrictions, the graph-support zero restrictions,
\(\max_i|(A_\star)_{ii}|\leq1-\gamma\),
\(\max_{i,j}|(A_\star)_{ij}|\leq L\), diagonality of \(D_\star\), and
\[
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq D_\star\preceq d_{\max}I_d.
\]
Consequently, on \(E_n\), every condition in
\(\mathrm{def{:}inverse\mbox{-}region}\) is satisfied by
\((A,D)=(A_\star,D_\star)\), with existential witnesses
\((M_0,M_1)=(M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\).  Hence
\[
 E_n\subseteq\{(A_\star,D_\star)\in\mathcal R_n\}.
\]
For every \(z\in\mathbb T\), the same stability margin ensures that
\[
 |1-(A_\star)_{vv}z|
 \geq 1-|(A_\star)_{vv}||z|
 \geq\gamma>0,
\]
so the target transfer is well defined.  By
\(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}confidence\mbox{-}set}\), the preceding
event inclusion implies
\[
 E_n\subseteq
 \left\{z\longmapsto
 \frac{(A_\star)_{vu}z}{1-(A_\star)_{vv}z}
 \in\mathcal C_n^h\right\}.
\]
The uniform moment coverage in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\) now gives
\[
 P_\star\{h_{uv}\in\mathcal C_n^h\}
 \geq P_\star(E_n)\geq1-\alpha.
\]
Because \(P_\star\) was arbitrary, this inequality is uniform over the
compact class.  The argument checks all inverse equations simultaneously
and nowhere selects a matrix-root branch or divides by a divided difference.

For the final assertion, let \((A^{(1)},D^{(1)})\) and
\((A^{(2)},D^{(2)})\) be two compatible compact-class members inducing the
same stationary coarse moment pair \((M_0,M_1)\), and suppose their queried
transfers \(h_{uv}^{(1)}\) and \(h_{uv}^{(2)}\) are unequal.  On
\[
 E_n^\circ:=\{(M_0,M_1)\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\},
\]
the coarse-law equations above and the compact-class restrictions apply to
each \(k\in\{1,2\}\), whence
\[
 (A^{(k)},D^{(k)})\in\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad k=1,2.
\]
The transfer-set definition therefore gives the pointwise inclusion
\[
 \{h_{uv}^{(1)},h_{uv}^{(2)}\}\subseteq\mathcal C_n^h
 \quad\text{on }E_n^\circ.
\]
Thus both attained, unequal transfers remain in the confidence set whenever
the common moment pair is in the moment box, which is precisely the stated
possible noncontraction.

Fix \(n\geq3\) and a law \(P\) in
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\).  On the
trajectory space \(\Omega_n=\mathbb R^{(n+1)d}\), equipped with its Borel
sigma-field, define
\[
 \widehat K_{\Sigma,n}:\Omega_n\longrightarrow(0,\infty),
 \qquad \widehat K_{\Sigma,n}(w):=K_\Sigma.
\]
This map is measurable because the inverse image of a Borel set is either
\(\Omega_n\) or the empty set.  Put
\(\Sigma_{n,P}:=\operatorname{Cov}_P(W_n)\).  The explicit uniform
resolvent bound in \(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\),
whose hypotheses are the restrictions collected in
\(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\), gives
\[
 \|\Sigma_{n,P}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq K_\Sigma.
\]
Since \(\Sigma_{n,P}\succeq0\), this is equivalent to
\[
 0\preceq\Sigma_{n,P}\preceq K_\Sigma I_{(n+1)d},
 \qquad
 \|\Sigma_{n,P}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\widehat K_{\Sigma,n}(W_n)
 \quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Thus the constant map is a simultaneous finite-sample covariance envelope.

It is also admissible for the spectral split in
\(\mathrm{def{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}handle}\).  Indeed, for
any symmetric lag-moment matrix \(H_{\ell ij}\), let
\(H_{\ell ij}=H_{\ell ij}^{+}-H_{\ell ij}^{-}\) be its positive and
negative spectral-part decomposition, with
\(H_{\ell ij}^{+},H_{\ell ij}^{-}\succeq0\).  For
\(s\in\{+,-\}\), covariance domination and cyclicity of trace give
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(H_{\ell ij}^{s}\Sigma_{n,P})
 =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(
 (H_{\ell ij}^{s})^{1/2}\Sigma_{n,P}
 (H_{\ell ij}^{s})^{1/2}\right)
 \leq K_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}(H_{\ell ij}^{s}).
\]
Submultiplicativity gives, in addition,
\[
 \|\Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}H_{\ell ij}^{s}
       \Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K_\Sigma\|H_{\ell ij}^{s}\|_{\mathrm{op}},
 \qquad
 \|\Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}H_{\ell ij}^{s}
       \Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm F}
 \leq K_\Sigma\|H_{\ell ij}^{s}\|_{\mathrm F}.
\]
Hence the trace, operator-norm, and Frobenius-norm quantities entering the
Gaussian quadratic-form calibration of both spectral parts are controlled
by the declared constant envelope.

For every realized trajectory, now set
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha):=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n:=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h:=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
For each \((\ell,i,j)\in\{0,1\}\times V\times V\), the corresponding
coordinate interval of \(\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)\) is therefore
identically
\[
 \operatorname{Out}_N\!\left((\widehat M_\ell)_{ij},
 2K_\Sigma\left\{
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^2/\alpha)}{n}}
 +\frac{\log(4d^2/\alpha)}{n}\right\}\right),
\]
the deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) interval in
\(\mathrm{def{:}moment\mbox{-}box}\).  Both intervals are produced by the
same invocation of \(\operatorname{Out}_N\); thus they have equal widths at
every sample point, irrespective of any excess width introduced by outward
rounding.  In particular,
\[
 P\!\left\{\text{all fallback coordinate widths are no larger than their
 deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) counterparts}\right\}=1.
\]
The equality of moment regions and
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\) imply
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})}
 P\{(M_0,M_1)\in\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)\}
 \geq1-\alpha.
\]
Every endpoint is rational by the defining guarantee of
\(\operatorname{Out}_N\).  Finally,
\(\widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n\) leaves all polynomial equalities
and inequalities of \(\mathrm{def{:}inverse\mbox{-}region}\) unchanged, and
\(\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h\) leaves the transfer projection
unchanged.  Hence the rational encoding and exact branch-free
semialgebraic inverse are preserved.  By
\(\mathrm{thm{:}global\mbox{-}honest\mbox{-}inversion}\), the same identities
also retain finite-sample transfer coverage.  Every width comparison used
above is an equality, so no strict adaptive improvement has been claimed.

For every \(n\geq3\), apply
\(\mathrm{thm{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}fallback}\).  Its
constant map \(w\mapsto K_\Sigma\) is measurable and is an admissible
covariance envelope for the positive and negative spectral parts.  The
theorem also gives, pointwise in the observed trajectory,
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
The first identity makes every coordinate interval exactly identical to its
deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) counterpart.  Hence the simultaneous
coordinatewise no-wider event has probability one under every compact-class
law for every \(n\).  Its probability therefore tends to one under every
interior regular law contained in that class.  The fallback theorem further
gives finite-sample moment coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) uniformly over the
compact class and proves that the rational outward rounding and exact
branch-free semialgebraic inverse are unchanged.  These conclusions prove
all parts of the statement.  Because the construction identifies the
adaptive region with the deterministic one, it certifies no strict adaptive
improvement.

theorem.statement:
The adaptive-calibration question has an affirmative answer in its literal
weak \emph{no wider} sense.  For every \(n\geq3\), choose in
\(\mathrm{CalHandle}\) the measurable constant covariance envelope
\(\widehat K_{\Sigma,n}\equiv K_\Sigma\) and set
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
For every compact-class law, every coordinate interval then has exactly the
width of its deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) counterpart with probability one.
Consequently the coordinatewise no-wider probability is one for every
\(n\), and hence tends to one for every interior regular law in that class.
The moment region has finite-sample coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) uniformly
over the compact class, its endpoints are rationally outward rounded, and
its exact branch-free semialgebraic inverse is preserved.  This construction
certifies equality of widths, not a strict adaptive improvement.
theorem.proof_tex:
Apply \(\mathrm{thm{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}fallback}\) for each
\(n\geq3\).  That theorem proves measurability and covariance domination for
the constant envelope and establishes the three displayed equalities of
random regions.  Equality of the moment regions makes each coordinate
interval identical, sample by sample, to its deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\)
counterpart.  The simultaneous no-wider event is therefore the whole
trajectory sample space and has probability one under every compact-class
law for every \(n\).  A constant sequence equal to one converges to one, in
particular under every interior regular law contained in the compact class.
The same fallback theorem supplies uniform finite-sample moment coverage,
rational outward rounding, and preservation of exact branch-free
semialgebraic inversion.  Since only equality of regions was used, this
argument entails no strict width reduction.

proofs.proof_tex:
Formally specialize Definitions~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} and~\texttt{def:certificate} to \(m=1\). Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\). The first equality in Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} gives
\[
B=A^1=A.
\]
The second equality in that definition and the identity \(A^0=I_d\) give
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{1-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
  =A^0D(A^0)^\top
  =D.
\]
Thus every compatible pair is \((B,Q)\), and the fiber has at most one element.

Conversely, substitute \((A,D)=(B,Q)\) into Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber}. The two coarse equalities hold because \(B^1=B\) and \(B^0Q(B^0)^\top=Q\). The remaining conditions in that definition hold if and only if
\[
B_{ij}=0\quad(i<j),
\qquad
B_{ij}=0\quad(i>j\text{ and }j\to i\notin G),
\]
\[
\max_i|B_{ii}|<1,
\qquad
Q_{ij}=0\quad(i\ne j),
\qquad
Q\succ0.
\]
These are exactly the fine-grid compatibility constraints obtained from Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} at \(m=1\). Hence
\[
\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=
\begin{cases}
\{(B,Q)\},&\text{if all of the displayed constraints hold},\\
\varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

It remains to verify the output of the exact algorithm in Definition~\texttt{def:certificate}. At \(m=1\), every enumerated diagonal-root equation is
\[
a_{ii}^{1}=B_{ii},
\]
so it has the unique real solution \(a_{ii}=B_{ii}\). The declared divided-difference polynomial satisfies
\[
C_1(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{0}x^r y^{0-r}=1.
\]
A nondecreasing walk of length one contains at most one strict increase. Therefore the indexing set defining every indirect-path remainder at \(m=1\) is empty, and in particular
\[
R_{vu,1}(A)=0.
\]
Consequently the graph-recursive root equation for the queried coordinate reduces to
\[
B_{vu}=A_{vu}C_1(A_{vv},A_{uu})+R_{vu,1}(A)=A_{vu};
\]
the identical argument applies to every permitted lower-triangular coordinate. Hence the recursion has the unique transition candidate \(A=B\). The coarse covariance equality then has the unique candidate \(D=Q\), as already shown directly above.

Because the compatibility and residual CAD tests in Definition~\texttt{def:certificate} are exact, they reject this candidate precisely when one of the defining fiber constraints fails. In that event the displayed fiber characterization gives \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\), so the certificate returns incompatibility. If all constraints hold, the algorithm accepts the unique compatible pair \((B,Q)\). The two-copy transfer-inequality system is then infeasible, because each copy must equal \((B,Q)\); the certificate therefore returns the common transfer. By the declared definition of \(h_{uv}\), that transfer is
\[
h_{uv}(z)
=\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z}.
\]
Admissibility gives \(|B_{vv}|<1\). Since \(z\in\mathbb T\) gives \(|z|=1\),
\[
|B_{vv}z|=|B_{vv}|<1,
\]
and therefore \(1-B_{vv}z\ne0\). Thus the returned rational function is well defined on \(\mathbb T\); because \(A=B\), it is exactly the unaliased direct fine-grid process transfer. This proves the proposition.
